title: Budget 2026: growth, gilt markets and choices for the Chancellor
label: 14 October 2026 · Budget 2026 evidence session
summary: Economists told the Treasury Committee that UK growth has been more resilient than expected, driven partly by global investment and AI, and that recent productivity data revisions are cautiously encouraging. They warned markets care most about near-term deficits and credible fiscal discipline, not headline 'headroom' figures; they urged protecting public investment and R&D, warned against ill‑timed tax rises (especially cap gains alignment), and urged clearer independent assessment of long-term infrastructure spending and stronger local capacity for devolution.

glossary.definition: UK government bonds; their yields show how much investors demand to lend to the government.
Office for Budget Responsibility, the UK's independent budget forecaster.
Capital Gains Tax, the tax on profits when someone sells an asset.
Capital expenditure—companies' spending on equipment, buildings and other long-term assets.
Gross value added per worker, a measure of output produced per employee (a productivity measure).
Shifting powers, funding or responsibilities from central government to regional or local bodies.

chapters.title: How the economy looks now
chapters.takeaway: The UK has been unexpectedly resilient this year, but forecasters differ and uncertainty is high.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're hearing evidence ahead of the Budget on 28 October. Let's start with the state of the UK economy and the impact of global events like the Iran war.

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: The UK's resilience has surprised us, but it's part of a global upswing—strong growth and investment in the US, Asia and Europe. Global drivers, not UK-only factors, explain much of it.

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Two big influences are an investment (capex) boom and higher equity and asset prices. That supports spending even with higher interest rates, but risks are large and outlooks uncertain.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: The IMF trimmed UK 2027 growth but the OBR is more optimistic—what's your view for next year?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Our baseline is slightly above 1%—not the 1.6% the OBR forecast. Trend growth in the UK looks closer to 1%.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: Recent quarters show growth above 2% in H1 2026. People doubt it because growth disappointed for years, but productivity appears to have improved recently too.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: The UK has performed well within the G7 this year. We must be cautious, but recent data revisions and a pickup in GVA per worker suggest encouraging signs.

chapters.title: Gilts, inflation and what markets care about
chapters.takeaway: Markets focus on near-term deficits and the Bank of England's policy path more than headline fiscal 'headroom'.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Gilt yields are high—why? Is it UK fiscal policy or global factors?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Mostly global factors: energy shocks and a global capex boom. UK short-term yields are high because markets expect the Bank of England to raise rates; fiscal credibility adds maybe ~20 basis points.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: From my checks, UK gilts haven't been hit more than other G7 bonds over the past year. Inflation outlook and expected Bank rate path matter most.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: If the Government uses the fiscal buffer now, will bond markets tolerate it?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Markets won't obsess over a small change in headroom. They look at near-term deficits and gilt issuance. Shrinking the deficit toward the low‑to‑mid 3% range next year would reassure markets.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: Is there a market price for specific headroom levels?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: No market instrument for 'headroom' itself—sell-side expectations are £10–£20 billion.

chapters.title: Productivity: data revisions and drivers
chapters.takeaway: Recent statistical revisions lift measured UK productivity; the pickup may be partly real and linked to investment and other changes.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Two big data changes improved our picture: better measurement of workers using PAYE data and new hours measures. GVA per worker and per hour look better than previously reported.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Between 2024 Q3 and 2026 Q2, GVA per worker rose 2.8%, annualised ~1.6%—close to pre-crisis per‑worker trends. The long-term slowdown since the financial crisis is smaller than we thought.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: So we restated 15–18 years of productivity history because of a new method?

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Yes—it's a measurement issue. That doesn't mean the UK's productivity problems are solved, but it's a better starting point.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: There's also a thought that labour-cost shocks—like employer national insurance rises—may have nudged firms to use labour more efficiently, helping measured productivity.

turns.speaker: Chris Coghlan
turns.text: Could another downturn limit policy room to respond?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: High debt reduces fiscal room. Expect the Bank of England to do more counter-cyclical work if the next downturn hits, because Governments have less space.

chapters.title: Fiscal choices: headroom, taxes and borrowing for investment
chapters.takeaway: Protect public investment and R&D, avoid ill-timed tax rises, and establish stronger independent scrutiny for big investments.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Should the Chancellor raise CGT or tax banks more to balance the books?

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: I would be cautious about raising CGT or undermining venture capital incentives—taxing risky investment like income. If numbers are needed, modest bank tax changes are less harmful than CGT alignment.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Avoid measures that raise business costs and damage investment. Public investment is the key margin for growth—protect and increase it.

turns.speaker: Chris Coghlan
turns.text: Could the Government credibly borrow more for infrastructure or R&D?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Borrowing more to invest would likely raise yields unless markets see immediate near-term fiscal improvement. The market cares first about the headline deficit and issuance.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: I don't advocate breaking the rules, but we need an independent 'OBR for infrastructure' to assess project returns and multipliers so markets and the public can trust borrowing for investment.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Public finance institutions (British Business Bank, National Wealth Fund) could scale up, but we need evidence-based assessment to show borrowing is justified and truly additional.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: Would ring‑fenced bonds for infrastructure help?

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: Possible, but what we really need is stronger independent scrutiny and clearer incentives—like nudging pensions toward UK investment—to unlock private capital.

chapters.title: Industrial strategy, R&D and regional growth
chapters.takeaway: Targeted industrial strategy and more public R&D are vital; devolved powers must be matched with local capacity and accountability.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: Does an active industrial strategy pick winners unfairly, or is it justified?

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Modern industrial strategy isn't just subsidies; it targets sectors where the UK has strengths and where public action removes barriers—skills, regulation, places and supply‑chain resilience.

turns.speaker: Chris Coghlan
turns.text: Should we borrow for R&D and aim to be top of the G7?

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: R&D delivers high returns. We can't match every country's scale, but we should protect and target public R&D, especially applied R&D that feeds growth and leverages our strengths.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: Public investment boards and finance arms should show more appetite and ambition. The public institutions should be tools to back real growth projects.

turns.speaker: Ms Minns
turns.text: You criticised 'growth in every postcode'—how should Government pick places to back?

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Use multiple data sources to identify real regional strengths and clusters, complement national evidence with local insight, then prioritise places where policy can remove clear barriers.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: Be selective. Reward places that show capacity and momentum, and tie money to accountability—devolution without capability or oversight will fail.

chapters.title: Devolution, accountability and what the Chancellor should do
chapters.takeaway: Sequence devolution to places with capacity, protect capital spending and send a clear signal of fiscal discipline; devolve adult skills to advanced mayoralties.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On devolution: would markets worry if mayors got tax shares without strong accountability?

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: Markets focus on national fiscals; they wouldn't micro-manage local accountability. But from a governance view, having accountability and capacity matters for outcomes.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: In principle, sharing income tax with mayors can work, but not overnight. Start with places that have the capacity and be strict about responsibilities and measurement.

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Sequence devolving powers to places with evidence-based plans and local capacity. Pair national institutions (UKRI, National Wealth Fund) with local partners for checks and scale.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: Quick question—what mistakes did the previous Chancellor make?

turns.speaker: Professor Valero
turns.text: Welfare reform proved politically hard to deliver quickly; some tax rises are growth-damaging, but securing a sustainable fiscal position also matters for long-run growth.

turns.speaker: Dr Beck-Friis
turns.text: From markets' eyes, avoid inflationary tax hikes and show near-term deficit reduction; that keeps gilt yields lower and preserves policy room.

turns.speaker: Lord O’Neill
turns.text: For me, the Chancellor should prioritise devolution with capacity-building, protect public investment, and avoid hasty tax measures that dent business confidence—especially CGT alignment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Committee will publish this transcript and use these points in our Budget work.
